newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat dives late as EU hikes export subsidy.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat dives late as EU hikes export subsidy.

text.p: A surprising hike in the EU's export subsidy for wheat and wheat flour plus a dismal weekly U.S. wheat export sales pace dropped CBOT wheat futures sharply lower on the close, traders said.
"The world market is weak. The EU stepped up their restitution to 13 Ecus per tonne, which is double," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for FIMAT Futures.

New lows were set, selling was broad-based and included commercial selling plus unwinding of CBOT/KCBT and CBOT/MGE wheat spreads, the traders said. The new low for March was $3.79, down from the previous low of $3.87-1/2 set Tuesday.

Grain exporters said EU officials in Brussels had awarded wheat export subsidies up to 13 Ecus per tonne for 290,000 tonnes of wheat, stretching into double figures for the first time this season and raising market competition another notch.

Wheat collapsed late with fund, commission house, local and commercial selling noted during the last 15 minutes of trading. Cargill Inc was a late seller of two million bushels of December, Refco Inc sold 2.5 million December and Tenco Inc sold one million December, traders said.
Wheat closed 1-1/2 to 14-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with December down 14-1/2 at $3.84.
Wheat tumbled late but was trading at lower levels in early dealings on dismal export sales data.
USDA early Thursday said U.S. net wheat exports for the week ended October 17 tallied 279,500 tonnes, down 62 percent from a week ago and 44 percent below the four-week average.
Further evidence that the world supply of wheat was increasing also lent pressure.
The International Grains Council (IGC) Thursday boosted its estimate for 1996 wheat production to 573 million tonnes from the previous 571 million.
"The sales report hurt and the IGC raised their estimate for wheat stocks worldwide and that didn't help any," a trader said.
Talk that Turkey may reject shipments of U.S. wheat was bearish, traders said.
